We developed the multisource fusion model for osteoporotic vertebral fracture (MSF-OVF), an interpretable source-aware framework integrating clinical-demographic variables, BMD, and lumbar MRI-derived ventral and dorsal paraspinal muscle (PM) representations. This retrospective multicenter study included 2680 participants aged > 40 years from five centers (one training, one internal validation, four external test cohorts). Deep features from four PM regions were extracted using vision foundation model-guided transfer learning and integrated with age, sex, body mass index, and BMD through source-aware latent fusion. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), calibration, and interpretability analyses. MSF-OVF achieved an AUC of 0.881 (95% CI, 0.854-0.909) in internal validation and 0.851-0.917 across four external cohorts. Compared with the clinical-demographic and BMD baseline, MSF-OVF improved AUC by 0.046-0.093 and significantly outperformed it in internal validation and most external cohorts (DeLong P ≤ 0.034). Continuous NRI was 0.268-1.034 across all validation cohorts (P ≤ 0.011). MSF-OVF also outperformed single-muscle models (AUC, 0.454-0.736; P ≤ 0.009). After training-derived logistic recalibration, the internal validation Brier score was 0.140, with a calibration-in-the-large (CITL) of - 0.168 and calibration slope of 0.926. Class activation maps mainly highlighted PM regions. Automated segmentation took several seconds and inference 57.71 ± 18.66 ms per participant. Source-aware fusion of clinical-demographic, BMD, and PM MRI information may support computer-aided multicenter OVF prediction.

articles.title: Deep Learning-Based Automated Computed Tomography Classification of Posterior Malleolar Fractures for a Standardized Diagnostic Framework.
articles.abstract: Despite advances in computed tomography (CT)-based classification systems for posterior malleolar fractures (PMFs), diagnostic consistency remains limited because these systems are still highly dependent on the observer's experience. This study aimed to develop a deep learning-based automated model capable of classifying PMFs according to the Haraguchi, Mason-Molloy, and Bartoníček-Rammelt clasification systems using CT scans, and to compare the classification performance of different convolutional neural network architectures. Retrospectively collected preoperative CT data from 480 adult patients with PMFs were analyzed. A total of 2398 CT slices were independently classified by three orthopedic surgeons according to the three classification systems, and majority consensus was used as the reference standard. Anonymized DICOM images were evaluated using VGG-16, ResNet-101, and DenseNet-121 architectures. The dataset was divided into 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% testing subsets. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, precision, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). The VGG-16 and ResNet-101 models demonstrated high classification performance in the Haraguchi and Mason-Molloy systems. In the VGG-16 model, AUC values exceeded 0.90 across most fracture subtypes, reaching particularly high levels in Haraguchi types I-III, Mason-Molloy types IIB and III, and Bartoníček-Rammelt type IV. Similarly, the ResNet-101 model achieved AUC values above 0.90 in most classes, with very high discriminative performance observed in selected subtypes. F1-scores were greater than 0.70 among most fracture categories and exceeded 0.80 in several, indicating strong and consistent classification performance. These findings demonstrate that deep learning-based automated CT classification of PMFs is feasible and diagnostically robust. The proposed framework may improve diagnostic consistency, reduce observer-dependent variability, and support standardized assessment of posterior malleolar fractures in clinical practice.

articles.title: CLIP-CGPNet: A Multimodal Clinical Decision Support System for Postoperative UTUC Recurrence Prediction.
articles.abstract: Accurate prediction of postoperative recurrence is essential for individualized management and follow-up planning in patients with upper tract urothelial carcinoma (UTUC). However, reliable risk stratification remains challenging due to the heterogeneous nature of imaging characteristics and clinical information. In this study, we propose a multimodal clinical decision support framework that integrates contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) images with routinely available clinical variables for postoperative recurrence prediction. The proposed framework adopts an image-clinical integrated learning strategy to enhance semantic alignment between visual representations and patient-specific clinical context. Imaging features are guided by clinically informed semantic prompts, while a dynamic fusion mechanism adaptively balances the contributions of different modalities. This design enables robust multimodal interaction and improves the individualized risk estimation. The framework is evaluated using a retrospective UTUC cohort of 160 patients treated between 2016 and 2023, including 59 recurrence cases and 101 nonrecurrence cases. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.87, demonstrating superior performance compared with conventional convolutional neural network-based models and representative multimodal baselines. Qualitative analyses further indicate improved alignment between imaging patterns and clinical factors, providing interpretable insights through attention-based visualization. These findings suggest that the proposed multimodal framework provides a potential approach for postoperative UTUC recurrence risk stratification and has the potential to support clinical decision-making and risk-adapted postoperative management.

articles.title: Comparison of the Performances of Deep Learning Methods in Kellgren-Lawrence Classification of Knee Osteoarthritis: A Multicenter Study.
articles.abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) causes symptoms such as pain, stiffness, and functional limitation in the knees; plain knee radiographs are used in addition to physical examination in its diagnosis. This study aimed to compare the performance of pre-trained deep learning models in knee OA classification and to examine the effects of lateral knee radiographs and patient clinical data on the performance of these models. Eight centers participated in the study; radiographs from six centers were used for training, validation, and testing of the models, and radiographs from two centers were used for external validation. In addition to anteroposterior (AP) and lateral knee radiographs, clinical information such as age, gender, height, and weight was collected from the patients. A total of 1550 patients were included in the study. The performance of deep learning models VGG-16, ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, Inception_v3, and EfficientNetb0 was compared in the classification of knee OA. The VGG-16 model yielded significantly higher performance metrics than competing architectures (p < 0.001), with an accuracy of 0.73, sensitivity of 0.72, specificity of 0.93, F1 score of 0.72, positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.72, quadratic weighted Kappa of 0.91, and AUC of 0.93. Feature extraction was performed using the VGG-16 model, and the patient's age, gender, and BMI clinical characteristics were added to the image feature set and classified using machine learning algorithms. The XGBoost classifier showed statistically insignificant improvements of 1-2% in performance metrics. Similar performance results were obtained with the VGG-16 model in a study using only AP knee radiographs. Radiographs from two centers were used for external validation, and the VGG-16 model yielded accuracy of 0.65, sensitivity of 0.65, specificity of 0.91, PPV of 0.67, F1 score of 0.65, quadratic weighted kappa of 0.88, and AUC of 0.90. Adding age, gender, and BMI clinical characteristics to the knee radiograph image feature set did not significantly improve model performance. Furthermore, adding lateral radiographs to the AP knee radiograph set did not provide any additional contribution to KL classification performance.

articles.title: HCF-Net: a Hierarchical Cascade Fusion Network Aligned with Clinical Treatment Pathways for Preoperative Molecular Subtyping of Breast Cancer on Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced MRI.
articles.abstract: Preoperative molecular subtyping of breast cancer is essential for treatment selection and prognosis assessment, yet most deep learning approaches formulate subtype prediction as a conventional flat multi-class task without reflecting the sequential clinical decision process. We developed HCF-Net, a hierarchical cascade fusion network that decomposes subtype prediction into three clinically aligned binary decision nodes and integrates multiphase DCE-MRI with clinicoradiologic information. The model was retrospectively developed and validated using a dual-center cohort of 373 women who underwent preoperative 3.0 T multiphase DCE-MRI. On an independent test set (n = 75), HCF-Net achieved a Macro-AUC of 0.868 (95% CI, 0.806-0.923), accuracy of 73.3%, Macro-F1 of 0.732, and Cohen's κ of 0.631. The fusion model consistently achieved the highest AUC across all three hierarchical decision nodes, reaching 0.890 for luminal versus non-luminal tumors, 0.865 for Luminal A versus Luminal B tumors, and 0.974 for HER2-enriched versus triple-negative tumors. The same ordering of classification strategies was observed with a ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone. Compared with conventional flat classification strategies, hierarchical cascade decomposition and decision-level fusion provided substantial performance gains. These findings suggest that a hierarchical fusion framework aligned with clinical decision pathways may provide an effective and interpretable approach for preoperative breast cancer molecular subtype prediction.

articles.title: Validation of a Deep Learning Model for Automated Ureteral Length Measurement on CT Against Gross Specimens.
articles.abstract: This study validates a deep learning model for automated ureteral length measurement on CT using gross specimen measurements as the reference standard. A deep learning model was trained on 3629 CT series from 1502 patients (cohort 1) to segment the ureter and extract centerline length. An independent prospective cohort (cohort 2) of 70 patients undergoing radical nephroureterectomy served as the hold-out test set. Each gross specimen was measured twice by one urologist (D1_length and D2_length), with their mean as the reference length (Ref_length). Model-predicted lengths (AI_length) were compared with Ref_length using repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests. Determinants of discrepancy were assessed with Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression. Marginal means (± SE) were 266 ± 3.85 mm (D1_length), 273 ± 3.25 mm (D2_length), 269 ± 2.75 mm (AI_length), and 269 ± 3.45 mm (Ref_length). Measurement method had a statistically significant but negligible effect on length (F(3, 207) = 2.73, p = 0.045, η2G = 0.007). D1_length and D2_length differed significantly from Ref_length (both p = 0.002), whereas AI_length was not statistically different from Ref_length (p > 0.999). In regression analysis, reference ureteral length was the only independently associated variable (coefficient - 0.54 mm per mm of reference length, 95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.39; p < 0.001); age, sex, body height, body weight, operation side, and lesion location were not significantly associated. The proposed deep learning pipeline achieved accurate fully automated ureteral segmentation and length measurement across diverse CT acquisition phases and demonstrated close agreement with surgical gross specimen measurements in a prospective clinical cohort, supporting its potential to assist preoperative planning and reduce reliance on manual measurement. The measurement discrepancy was governed primarily by ureteral length itself-with a small systematic underestimation in longer ureters-rather than by patient or procedural factors. However, this tendency, together with the single-center design, and the modest size of the prospective cohort, warrants further multicenter validation before routine clinical deployment.

articles.title: AI-based Hip Fracture Classification from Pelvic X-ray Images Using a Hybrid PEFT-ViT and XGBoost Model.
articles.abstract: Accurate radiographic classification of hip fractures into femoral neck (intracapsular) versus intertrochanteric (extracapsular) types is essential for surgical planning, yet most AI studies focus on binary detection using large datasets from high-resource regions, with no prior work from the Middle East. This study proposes a Hybrid PEFT-ViT and XGBoost framework for three-class classification of hip radiographs (Normal, Intertrochanteric fracture, Neck of femur fracture), using 768 X-ray images collected from King Abdullah University Hospital (KAUH) in Northern Jordan. A LoRA-fine-tuned ViT-Base/16 backbone extracted fused class-token and patch-token features, which were classified using XGBoost. On an independent test set of 77 radiographs, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 88.31% (95% CI 79.3-93.7%), a sensitivity of 87.75%, a specificity of 94.28%, and an F1-score of 87.75%, the highest among the evaluated CNN-based (MobileNetV2, DenseNet121) and transformer-based (ViT, DeiT, Swin) baselines. These results show that clinically meaningful hip fracture classification can be achieved using a single-center dataset, providing a practical framework for resource-limited settings, although external validation is still required.

articles.title: Explainability and Clinical Trust of Deep Learning in Glioblastoma Treatment Efficacy Prediction: A Comprehensive Framework.
articles.abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) treatment response is highly heterogeneous. Predicting outcomes from pre-treatment MRI is a critical unmet need, yet the clinical adoption of "black box" deep learning (DL) models is hindered by a lack of transparency. Robust and holistic validation frameworks still need to be developed to allow clinical trust. A multi-layered eXplainable AI (XAI) pipeline was employed to dissect a previously developed deep learning model trained to predict GBM overall survival. First, the model's visual focus was qualitatively and quantitatively analysed. Second, the model's feature dependence was quantified using input ablation studies. Third, the depth at which class information becomes decodable was traced by linear probing of the internal representations. Finally, the clinical impact of the AI and its explanations was assessed in a multi-reader, multi-case study (37 patients, 4 readers, 3 phases, 444 observations) using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) and clustered bootstrapping. Analysis revealed a high-intensity heuristic: hyper-intense pixels at the skull periphery anchored "Long-Term" predictions, while the model defaulted to "Short-Term" based on tumour enhancement in its absence. The ablation study established this dependence, and linear probing pointed in the same direction. In the clinical study, AI assistance significantly improved expert accuracy (OR 1.598, p < 0.01) without artificially boosting confidence (p = 0.561). Importantly, the addition of XAI heatmaps was associated with a change in how experts used the AI score (interaction p < 0.01), and with fewer patients wrongly called long-term survivors. High predictive accuracy can mask reliance on low-level intensity heuristics. While superficial interpretation of saliency maps is perilous, multi-layered audits expose these shortcuts. Clinically, spatial heatmaps were associated with improved expert diagnostic accuracy and a shift in decision-making strategy.

articles.title: Cross-Dataset Reliability of Deep Learning Models for Pressure Injury Staging: a Multiarchitecture Evaluation and Prediction-Error Analysis.
articles.abstract: Deep learning models have been proposed for automated pressure injury staging, but reliability across external wound image datasets remains uncertain. This study assessed cross-dataset reliability across multiple architectures. After dataset curation, including duplicate-image screening, 1081 images from the Pressure Injury Image Dataset (PIID), 1844 images from an institutional Hallym University Medical Center (HUMC) dataset, and 141 Kaggle images were analyzed. Six convolutional neural network and Transformer architectures were trained on PIID or HUMC and evaluated on internal and external datasets without additional fine-tuning or threshold adjustment. The primary outcome was the internal-to-external generalization gap in macro-averaged F1 score. Models trained on PIID achieved a mean internal macro-averaged F1 score of 0.75, decreasing to 0.36 on HUMC and 0.56 on Kaggle. Models trained on HUMC achieved a mean internal macro-averaged F1 score of 0.66, decreasing to 0.53 on both external datasets. No architecture consistently outperformed others in external validation. Prediction-error analysis showed dataset-dependent differences in error direction. Understaging and overstaging errors were defined as predictions below and above the true stage. Models trained on PIID predominantly produced understaging errors on HUMC, and models trained on HUMC predominantly produced overstaging errors on PIID. Exploratory analysis of frozen feature vectors showed limited grouping of images in feature space, with dataset source more closely associated with feature structure than pressure injury stage. These findings support the importance of cross-dataset validation in evaluating automated pressure ulcer staging models. The observed performance degradation and dataset-dependent error patterns suggest sensitivity to dataset-level heterogeneity. Consequently, this study supports two important points. First, in the field of pressure ulcers where image capture protocols are not fixed, external validation using diverse datasets is necessary to evaluate generalization performance. Second, a unified protocol must be included in the data acquisition process to develop reproducible models.

articles.title: Can General-purpose Multimodal AI Reliably Measure Cobb Angles? A Head-to-head Diagnostic Agreement Study of GPT-5.1 and Gemini 3.1 Pro in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis.
articles.abstract: General-purpose multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) models can interpret radiographs through natural-language prompts, but their quantitative agreement and anatomical traceability in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis remain uncertain. We compared GPT-5.1 and Gemini 3.1 Pro with a joint expert-consensus reference on 125 anonymized standing coronal whole-spine radiographs. Each model evaluated each image once in an independent chat session using the same standardized prompt; only the first response was retained. Outcomes included single-measure absolute-agreement intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), mean absolute error (MAE) relative to the reference, Bland-Altman analysis, error-threshold performance, categorical agreement, and end-vertebra concordance. Gemini 3.1 Pro showed higher ICC (0.842 versus 0.587), lower mean bias (3.46° versus 8.68°), lower MAE (5.06° versus 9.62°; paired P < 0.001), and more measurements within 5° of the reference (61.6% versus 24.8%). Agreement with reference categories was 80.0% versus 52.8% for angle-derived severity and 78.4% versus 52.8% for prompt-constrained management categories (both paired P < 0.001). Exact upper end-vertebra agreement was 14.4% versus 8.8%, and exact lower end-vertebra agreement was below 20% for both models. Gemini 3.1 Pro performed better under the tested single-session protocol, but neither model demonstrated sufficient case-level agreement and end-vertebra concordance to support autonomous Cobb-angle measurement. These results are relative to expert consensus and do not establish absolute measurement accuracy or model repeatability. Expert verification remains necessary.

articles.title: Reproducibility and diagnostic performance of ADC for assessing response to neoadjuvant immunotherapy in muscle-invasive bladder cancer: a multi-ROI comparison analysis from the phase-Ib NABUCCO trial.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: MRI is increasingly used to assess treatment response in muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC), but only qualitatively. This study evaluates the reproducibility and predictive value of quantitative apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), thought to be a non-invasive surrogate for tumor cell density, in patients with MIBC receiving neoadjuvant immunotherapy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: MRI data from 35 patients, enrolled in the Phase-Ib NABUCCO trial, were analyzed. ADC maps were derived from pre- and post-treatment MRI scans. Three independent radiologists assessed multiple regions of interest (ROIs) to evaluate inter-observer agreement and predictive performance for pathological complete response (pCR). ADC values were normalized using muscle tissue as a reference. Additionally, we analyzed the correlation between ADC and cell densities, derived from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF) data. RESULTS: ADC measurements from the whole-tumor ROI (n = 25) demonstrated the highest reproducibility (0.98, 95% CI = [0.95-0.99]), but lacked predictive value (AUC = 0.31, 95% CI = [0.12-0.53], p = 0.109). The most hypointense ROI (n = 22) showed the strongest predictive value for pCR (AUC = 0.80, 95% CI = [0.57-1], p = 0.025), though with limited reproducibility. The difference between baseline and follow-up ADC values in the hypointense region (n = 20) again showed the highest diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.80, 95% CI = [0.58-0.98], p = 0.015). Although muscle normalization is proposed to reduce scanner variability, it did not improve predictive performance in this cohort and occasionally reduced reproducibility. No significant correlation was found between whole-tumor ADC and cell density. CONCLUSION: Despite analyzing different measurement techniques for ADC values, none was simultaneously reproducible and predictive, nor provided insights into the biology of the tumor. While ADC shows promise in MIBC, there is an urgent need for more standardized, robust imaging biomarkers. KEY POINTS: Question Non-invasive biomarkers are urgently needed to guide bladder-preserving strategies in MIBC. Findings DWI-MRI shows promise, but standardized robust imaging biomarkers are essential for reliable response assessment. Critical relevance statement Standardized or AI-assisted ROI segmentation could improve ADC reproducibility and diagnostic accuracy in multicenter studies.

articles.title: RAPID perfusion CT in acute ischemic stroke: an educational pictorial review of common patterns, pearls, and pitfalls.
articles.abstract: Rapid processing of Perfusion and Diffusion (RAPID) software for CT perfusion (CTP) is a valuable tool for the evaluation of acute ischemic stroke and therapeutic decision-making in extended therapeutic windows. However, automated maps should not be interpreted in isolation. A structured, pattern-based approach, integrating qualitative visual assessment with automated quantitative output and clinical information to refine therapeutic selection, remains essential to mitigate pitfalls and optimize patient care. The aim of this article is to provide an educational pictorial review based on selected illustrative cases of the most common imaging patterns, interpretive pitfalls, and technical features of CTP processed with RAPID software in acute ischemic stroke, that may serve as a practical guide for radiologists and neuroradiologists. KEY POINTS: Question How can radiologists effectively interpret automated RAPID CT perfusion maps in acute ischemic stroke while avoiding common technical traps, diagnostic pitfalls, and anatomical limitations? Findings Integrating qualitative visual assessment, quantitative RAPID outputs, and clinical-vascular data within a structured workflow minimizes diagnostic errors and optimizes patient selection for reperfusion. Critical relevance statement This educational pictorial review provides a practical, pattern-based approach to RAPID CT perfusion interpretation, highlighting clinical applications, technical limitations, software variability, and diagnostic pitfalls to advance everyday neuroradiological practice and personalized stroke management.

articles.title: A rare case of bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions.
articles.abstract: Cuboid-navicular coalitions are an exceptionally rare form of tarsal coalitions, representing less than 1% of all tarsal coalitions. Although tarsal coalitions classically become symptomatic during adolescence, cuboid-navicular coalitions may remain clinically silent until adulthood and can present with nonspecific chronic midfoot or hindfoot pain. We present a rare case of bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions in a 42-year-old man with progressive bilateral midfoot pain, associated degenerative hindfoot and midfoot changes, and bilateral peroneal tendon pathology. Initial management consisted of orthotics, bracing, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, but symptoms progressed over 8 years. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated bilateral cuboid-navicular coalitions, progressive degenerative changes, and high-grade right peroneus longus tear. The patient underwent excision of the right cuboid-navicular coalition, excision of the right lateral calcaneal tubercle with inferior peroneal retinacular release, and debridement and repair of the right peroneus longus and brevis tendons. This case highlights the importance of considering rare tarsal coalitions in adults with chronic nonspecific midfoot pain and emphasizes the value of MRI and CT for diagnosis, characterization of associated pathology, and operative planning.

articles.title: Endovascular Therapy for Femoropopliteal Artery Lesions Involving the Popliteal Artery: 1-Year Outcomes from a Real-World Multicenter Registry.
articles.abstract: PURPOSE: To evaluate real-world outcomes of endovascular treatment for femoropopliteal lesions involving the popliteal artery and, in a post-hoc exploratory analysis, assess whether anatomical location (P3 vs. P1/P2 segments) was associated with clinical decision-making and prognosis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective, post-hoc analysis of 946 patients from the prospective PROMISING registry. For this exploratory analysis, patients were stratified according to distal (P3) versus proximal/mid (P1/P2) popliteal artery involvement. Predictors of stent implantation and clinical decision pathways were compared across groups. RESULTS: Overall procedural success was 98.5%, and the 12-month freedom from major adverse events (MAE), defined as a composite of all-cause mortality, major amputation, or clinically driven target lesion revascularization, was 80.1%. Multivariable analysis indicated P3 involvement independently predicted reduced stent implantation (OR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46-0.95, p = 0.027). For vessel preparation, the P3 group more frequently utilized plain old balloon angioplasty (POBA, 67.8% vs. 54.8%, p < 0.001) rather than directional atherectomy or specialty balloons. Despite a lower stent implantation rate and greater use of POBA, 12-month freedom from MAE was comparable between the P3 and P1/P2 groups (78.0% vs. 81.2%, p = 0.481). CONCLUSION: In this post-hoc analysis of real-world registry data, popliteal lesion location was associated with differences in operator treatment strategies. P3 involvement was associated with less frequent stent implantation and greater use of plain balloon angioplasty, while 1-year clinical outcomes were comparable between the P3 and P1/P2 groups. These exploratory findings require external validation before they can be used to inform clinical treatment strategies. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT04826705 (Registered on March 29, 2021).

articles.title: Motion uncertainty visualization based on Gaussian process regression.
articles.abstract: In the context of image-guided soft-tissue intervention and surgery navigation, soft tissue motion estimation for a deformed/registered pre-operative/pre-interventional medical image may suffer from multiple sources of uncertainty. Visualizing the uncertainty in the deformed image is of great interest because it conveys the uncertainty in the registered pre-interventional/pre-operative navigation information on deformable soft-tissue organs governing the decisions of the surgeon or intervention specialist. We address the problem of propagating the uncertainty from a Gaussian process (GP)-based motion estimation of an input image. To visualize the deformed image itself, we show its maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate. To convey the overall uncertainty in the MAP deformed image estimate, we apply a spatially-varying blur (according to the uncertain motion estimate) to an image containing a grid and combine it with the MAP deformed image itself. We show 2D cross sections of the final image that convey both the deformed image and its uncertainty. We further extend our approach to local investigations of points or regions of interest (e.g., a tumor). To visualize where a point/region of interest (POI/ROI) is after deformation, we estimate marginal (i.e., per voxel) label (e.g., for being a tumor) probabilities (MLPs) based on an input probabilistic segmentation of the ROI in the non-deformed pre-interventional/pre-operative image and the input GP posterior distribution over deformation fields and show 2D cross sections of visually mapped MLPs or MLP isocontours.

articles.title: De-Seg: Advancing OCTA segmentation with multi-scale feature fusion and edge refinement.
articles.abstract: Accurate segmentation of retinal vessels in optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) is essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of ocular diseases such as diabetic retinopathy and glaucoma. However, this task remains challenging due to the presence of low-contrast microvessels, projection artifacts, and interference from fine vessel structures. To overcome these limitations, we propose De-Seg, a deep learning framework designed to enhance vessel segmentation through multi-scale feature fusion and edge refinement. The model employs a dual-branch encoder that combines a U-Net-style backbone with parallel multi-scale convolutions and a dedicated edge-aware branch utilizing Sobel operators. These branches are effectively fused via skip-connected decoder layers to maintain high spatial precision. The bottleneck is augmented with a multi-layer perceptron (MLP) to capture global contextual information, while a Multi-Scale Feature Extraction Block (MS Block) enlarges the receptive field to better capture faint capillaries. An Edge Block is introduced to enhance boundary clarity and mitigate interference from lesion regions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that De-Seg achieves competitive performance on multiple OCTA benchmarks, yielding Dice scores of 92.13% on OCTA-3M and 94.67% on ROSSA, outperforming recent state-of-the-art methods. Ablation studies validate the necessity of each component in improving feature representation and edge accuracy. The framework exhibits strong generalization capability, showing robust performance even under cross-domain settings. Overall, De-Seg provides a reliable and efficient solution for quantitative OCTA analysis, with potential applicability to other vascular imaging modalities.

articles.title: Beyond the underuse of advanced imaging in clinical radiology: reasons, barriers, and lessons learned from whole-body MRI.
Fluent but not fail-safe: machine-translated radiology reports still need expert review.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cross-border care, teleradiology, and international referral pathways increasingly require radiology report translation, but isolated mistranslations may alter clinical meaning. We evaluated German-to-English machine translation of radiology reports and correction-based localization of text requiring review. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this retrospective study, 310 de-identified German radiology reports from June and July 2025 were translated into English with DeepL. Eight radiologists assigned 5-point quality scores and corrected perceived errors. Thirty reports were reviewed by all eight readers, and 280 reports were assigned for single-reader evaluation, yielding 520 evaluations. Automated metrics and large language model judges were tested for report-level identification of translations requiring review; a correction-based segment-level edit-prediction model was evaluated on held-out shared reports. RESULTS: Most translations were rated good or excellent (339/520, 65.2%), but clinically important mistranslations involved diagnosis, anatomy, and radiologic terminology. Agreement was low for ordinal quality scores (Krippendorff α = 0.078, p = 0.006) but high for expert corrections (pairwise "bilingual evaluation understudy"-BLEU = 83.0, p < 0.001). In the conservative primary screen of 30 shared reports, no automated method discriminated translations requiring review (area under receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC] = 0.51-0.65; p = 0.100-0.920). The final edit-prediction model achieved a concordance index of 0.697 and an AUC of 0.731 for segments edited by at least six of eight readers. CONCLUSION: Machine-translated radiology reports were often acceptable on average, but translations containing errors requiring expert review persisted. Expert corrections were more reproducible than ordinal quality scores and supported localization of text requiring human review. KEY POINTS: Question Cross-border radiology workflows increasingly require report translation, but fluent machine translations may still contain meaning-changing errors requiring expert review for safe care. Findings Most machine translations were rated good or excellent, yet clinically important mistranslations occurred, and automated report-level metrics did not reliably identify reports needing review. Relevance statement Machine translation may support cross-border radiology workflows, but clinically important mistranslations in otherwise fluent reports require human-in-the-loop oversight and tools that localize text requiring expert review.

articles.title: Development and independent regional validation of a dynamic ultrasound appendicitis score for suspected acute appendicitis: a prospective multicenter study.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical emergency. Although CT is highly accurate, radiation exposure is a major concern in children, young adults, and pregnant women. Ultrasound is radiation-free but operator-dependent, and current scores rely on static weights without accounting for important patient-finding interactions. OBJECTIVE: To develop and independently validate a Dynamic Ultrasound Appendicitis Score (Dynamic UAS) with interaction effects to improve risk stratification and potentially avoid unnecessary CT examinations. METHODS: A prospective multicenter study collected development (n = 802) and independent regional external validation (n = 262) data. The Dynamic UAS was derived using multivariable logistic regression with interaction terms and internally validated using bootstrapping (1000 resamples). RESULTS: A web-based calculator was developed. A sensitivity analysis addressed limitations of the reference standard, non-visualized appendix, and missing data. Appendicitis prevalence was 33.3% (development) and 32.8% (validation). The Dynamic UAS performed excellently in diagnosing acute appendicitis (AUC 0.96 and 0.94) and outperformed known scores (AUC 0.81 to 0.91). At the ≥ 6 level, sensitivity was 91.7%/90.7%, and specificity was 97.1%/96.0%. Calibration was good (slope 0.89, Brier 0.098). In non-visualized appendix cases, the AUC was 0.89 (95% CI: 0.84 to 0.93) in the external validation cohort and 0.90 (95% CI: 0.85 to 0.94) in the development cohort. The model is not very useful for distinguishing complicated from uncomplicated appendicitis (AUC 0.72). CONCLUSIONS: The Dynamic UAS is a novel, independently validated tool that may reduce unnecessary CT use in radiation-sensitive populations and resource-limited settings. Future studies in different international settings are needed.

CDPDNet: Integrating text guidance with hybrid vision encoders for medical image segmentation.
articles.abstract: Most publicly available medical segmentation datasets are only partially labeled, with annotations provided for a subset of anatomical structures. When multiple datasets are combined for training, this incomplete annotation poses challenges, as it limits the model's ability to learn shared anatomical representations among datasets. Furthermore, vision-only frameworks often struggle to resolve semantic ambiguities between missing labels and target regions, potentially hindering discriminative performance and cross-dataset consistency. In this study, we proposed a CLIP-DINO Prompt-Driven Segmentation Network (CDPDNet), which combined a self-supervised vision transformer with CLIP-based text embedding and introduced task-specific text prompts to tackle these challenges. Specifically, the framework was constructed upon a convolutional neural network (CNN) and incorporated DINOv2 to extract both fine-grained and global visual features, which were then fused using a multi-head cross-attention module to overcome the limited long-range modeling capability of CNNs. In addition, CLIP-derived text embeddings were projected into the visual space to help model complex relationships among organs and tumors. To further address the partial label challenge and enhance inter-task discriminative capability, a Text-based Task Prompt Generation (TTPG) module that generated task-specific prompts was designed to guide the segmentation. Extensive experiments on multiple medical imaging datasets demonstrated that CDPDNet consistently outperformed existing state-of-the-art segmentation methods. Code and pretrained model are available at: https://github.com/wujiong-hub/CDPDNet.git.

articles.title: RADMorph: A region-aware deformable registration network for organ-specific thoracic CT alignment.
articles.abstract: Deformable image registration plays an important role in radiation therapy, supporting applications such as contour propagation, treatment planning, and motion analysis. However, accurate registration of lung CT images remains challenging in the presence of large respiratory-induced deformations. In this study, we propose RADMorph, a deep learning framework that explicitly models region-dependent motion to improve registration robustness and anatomical consistency under large deformations. RADMorph comprises two key components. The Adaptive Region Feature Encoder (ARFE) learns region-specific motion representations through feature clustering and region-conditioned filtering, while the Region-Centered Displacement Modulator (RCDM) estimates deformation fields by integrating local image similarity with inter-region distance-based modulation. We evaluated RADMorph on multi-center datasets acquired under free-breathing and deep-inspiration breath-hold conditions, as well as on four-dimensional CT datasets. Across these datasets, RADMorph showed competitive overall performance compared with convolutional and transformer-based registration methods, with improvements varying across geometric and intensity-based metrics. The proposed method improved contour propagation and boundary localization for clinically relevant structures in most evaluated settings while reducing global deformation folding. Quantitative evaluations further demonstrated accurate voxel-level correspondence across the evaluated datasets, supporting the potential use of RADMorph in applications that rely on spatial correspondence, such as dose mapping and adaptive radiotherapy. RADMorph integrates region-aware representation learning with distance-modulated deformation estimation to provide a region-informed approach for modeling complex respiratory motion. These characteristics may facilitate more reliable contour transfer and quantitative analysis of dynamic thoracic imaging.
